title: Acedia and Vainglory
english: A well-rooted tree was not shaken by the violence of winds, and acedia did not bend a firmly-supported soul. A wandering monk is brushwood of the desert; he rested a little, and is carried along again unwillingly. A transplanted plant bears no fruit, and a wandering monk will produce no fruit of virtue. A sick man is not content with one food, and an acedia-stricken monk [is not content] with one work. One woman will not suffice for a lover of pleasure, and one cell will not suffice for an acedia-stricken monk.

Chapter 14. The eye of the acedia-stricken stares intently at the windows, and his mind imagines those who visit; the door creaked, and he leapt up; he heard a voice, and peeped through the little window, and does not leave it until he grows numb sitting there. An acedia-stricken reader yawns repeatedly, and is easily carried toward sleep; he rubs his face, stretches his hands, turns his eyes from the book and stares at the wall; turning back again he read a little, and unfolding it pries into the ends of the chapters, counts the pages, tallies the quires, finds fault with the writing and its ornament; and afterward, folding it, he put the book under his head and sleeps a sleep not very deep — for hunger then wakes his soul and attends to its own concerns. An acedia-stricken monk is reluctant toward prayer, and will never utter words of prayer; for just as a sick man cannot bear a heavy burden, so the acedia-stricken will not do God’s work diligently; for the one has been deprived of the strength of his body, and the other has had the sinews of his soul loosened. Endurance heals acedia, as does doing all things with much persistence and the fear of God. Set a measure for yourself in every work, and do not depart before you complete it, and pray sensibly and vigorously, and the spirit of acedia will flee from you.

Chapter 15. On vainglory. Vainglory is an irrational passion, and easily entwines itself with every work of virtue. A line drawn on water is confounded, and the labor of virtue [is confounded] in a vainglorious soul. A hand covered by the bosom has become white, and a hidden deed shines more brightly than light.
